item.title: TrackMe - v2.4.22 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
**TrackMe 2.4.22 — Splunk S2S and Splunk UF Fleet, two new tenant types for Splunk forwarding, and User Activity Monitoring Data usage: who reads which index, and what the unread data costs.** * **Splunk S2S and Splunk UF Fleet.** Two new dedicated tenant types monitor how a Splunk deployment forwards its data, from what Splunk already writes: nothing is installed on a forwarder and nothing new is ingested. Splunk S2S watches the receivers, intermediate forwarders and pools (an indexer cluster is a pool, one per site of a multisite cluster, and the intermediate forwarders are grouped by host-name family), their traffic and their TLS and acknowledgement posture. Splunk UF Fleet follows the forwarding agents, their groups and the Deployment Servers that manage them. Both bring the findings model of the other dedicated tenants, with their own AI Agent. See [Splunk S2S](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/splunk_s2s.html#splunk-s2s) and [Splunk UF Fleet](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/splunk_uf_fleet.html#splunk-uf-fleet). * **User Activity Monitoring: Data usage.** Every audited search is resolved to the indexes it actually reads, through its knowledge objects, and weighed with the volume and cost of each index: globally, per index, per account and per knowledge object. An index is only called unread when the evidence supports it. See [Data usage](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/components_uam.html#pg-components-uam-data-usage). * **VOL: exact license figures.** Late license events are never lost, closed license days are reconciled against Splunk’s own Usage records with every difference explained, and volumes use binary units by default. See [Volume Outliers](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/components_vol.html#pg-components-vol). * **Cribl Edge and Cribl Stream.** Cribl Edge gains object monitoring with activity trends; Cribl Stream routes, pipelines and destinations open with their connected objects. See [Cribl Edge](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/cribl_edge.html#cribl-edge) and [Cribl Stream](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/components_cribl.html#pg-components-cribl). * **Every findings tenant.** Custom policies can drive findings actions and automations, links in notifications use a configurable Splunk Web root URL, and searches trust Splunk’s own job state, so a busy or restarting indexer no longer causes re-reads. See [Findings actions](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/findings.html#pg-findings-actions). * **Workload.** Entities whose scheduled search was deleted from Splunk are flagged and retired automatically. See [Workload](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/components_wlk.html#pg-components-wlk). * **Reliability and compatibility.** Lighter User Activity Monitoring on large search head clusters, restore of deleted findings tenants, a clearer Configuration Guardian, Splunk 9.x TLS contexts, the openai SDK 3.x, and a DOMPurify security update. See: [https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/releasenotes.html#version-2-4-22-build-1793748743-03-11-2026](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/releasenotes.html#version-2-4-22-build-1793748743-03-11-2026)

item.title: Absolute Secure Endpoint SIEM Events and Inventory Add-on - v1.0.2 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Renamed to "Absolute Secure Endpoint SIEM Events and Inventory Add-on". No other changes: the app ID stays TA-absolute-secure-endpoint, so upgrades, accounts, inputs and checkpoints are not affected.


Short Description:
Collects Absolute Secure Endpoint SIEM events (device, console and alert activity) and device inventory from the Absolute API, with CIM mappings (Authentication, Change, Alerts, Data Access, Inventory) and an ES asset lookup. Accounts, inputs and status are managed in Splunk Web. Independent project, not affiliated with Absolute Software.


Description:
Collects Absolute Secure Endpoint data from the Absolute API and maps it to the Splunk Common Information Model. - SIEM events (sourcetype absolute:events): what devices report (applications installed, removed and updated; hardware, network, OS and user changes; location and geofence changes; encryption, antivirus and application-persistence status), what console users do (sign-ins, account and role changes, rules, geofences, policy groups, device freeze, disable and unenroll, location lookups), and alerts (alert rules that fired, connections blocked in restricted regions). The same events Absolute's SIEM Connector sends to a syslog server, read straight from the API, with each event's id and as JSON. - Devices (sourcetype absolute:devices): an inventory snapshot, one event per device: hardware, OS, users, agent, addresses, encryption, antivirus, location. CIM: Authentication, Change (Account_Management, Endpoint_Changes), Alerts, Data Access and Inventory. A saved search builds an Enterprise Security asset lookup from the device inventory. - Inputs page in Splunk Web: Absolute accounts (API host, token ID and secret key, optional proxy; stored encrypted in Splunk's credential store; a Test button checks the token) and inputs: add, edit, enable, disable, run now, delete. - SIEM events are collected from a checkpoint in overlapping windows and de-duplicated by event id: restarts and failures do not lose events. If Splunk stops a run part-way (input disabled or restarted), the next run continues from the checkpoint; at most the window it was cut off in is sent again. - Status dashboard: last run, events and devices collected, minutes behind, errors, how late events arrive. Overview dashboard: event types, console activity, alerts, posture changes, devices by OS, agent, encryption and antivirus. - Python standard library only, no third-party packages. Independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Absolute Software. Absolute and Absolute Secure Endpoint are trademarks of Absolute Software Corporation.

item.title: eStreamer Add-on for Cisco Secure Firewall (FMC/Firepower) - v2.2.2 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Renamed to "eStreamer Add-on for Cisco Secure Firewall (FMC/Firepower)". No other changes: the app ID stays TA-fmc-estreamer, so upgrades, inputs, certificates and bookmarks are not affected.


Short Description:
High-volume collector for Cisco Secure Firewall (FMC) connection events over eStreamer. Indexes them as cisco:sfw:estreamer with the Cisco Security Cloud app's field names, so its CIM mappings and dashboards work. Inputs, certificates and status are managed in Splunk Web. Independent project, not affiliated with Cisco.


Description:
Collects connection events from a Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) over eStreamer and indexes them as sourcetype cisco:sfw:estreamer, with the field names the Cisco Security Cloud app uses for that sourcetype (InitiatorIP, ResponderIP, FirewallRule, AC_RuleAction, ...). That app's field aliases, CIM mappings and dashboards therefore work on these events, and existing searches keep working. Busy FMCs send thousands of connection events per second. This add-on is built for that volume: each input decodes in parallel processes, keeps events on disk until Splunk has read them, and resumes from a bookmark after a restart, so a restart does not skip events. - One input per FMC, several FMCs per heavy forwarder - Inputs page in Splunk Web: add, edit, enable, disable and restart inputs, and upload the eStreamer client certificate (the PKCS12 file from the FMC, or PEM). Certificates are stored encrypted in Splunk's credential store. - Status dashboard: throughput, minutes behind the FMC, connects and errors, indexed volume and index delay per FMC - Names from the FMC's metadata: rules, access control policy (FirewallPolicy), prefilter policy (PrefilterPolicy), tunnel/prefilter rule (TunnelRule), zones, interfaces, devices, applications, URL categories and countries - host is a name you choose for each FMC; the FMC's address is in every event as SourceHost - Disk buffer with a size cap: files are deleted once Splunk has read them; when the buffer is full, delete the oldest files or pause - Python standard library only, no third-party packages Connection events only. Intrusion, file/malware and packet events can come from the Cisco Security Cloud app. Independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Cisco. Cisco, Cisco Secure Firewall, Firepower and FMC are trademarks of Cisco Systems, Inc.

item.title: TA-IPMI - v1.0.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Short Description:
Free server BMC monitoring for Splunk. Streams IPMI sensors (temps, fan RPM, volts, watts), chassis/PSU status, and the System Event Log from ipmitool's local interface into events and metrics, with Overview and Metrics dashboards. Passes AppInspect cloud pre-cert. Commercial use requires license.


Description:
TA-IPMI is a free, source-available Splunk add-on that brings out-of-band hardware health monitoring to any Splunk host with a server-class BMC. It reads full IPMI telemetry via ipmitool's local open interface and indexes it three ways with zero manual configuration: 1. Sensor readings: every SDR sensor (temperatures, fan RPM, voltages such as 12V/3.3V/Vcore/BAT, power draw in watts, plus thresholds), plus chassis and BMC status as rich JSON events (index=main, sourcetype ipmi:status) for fielded search. 2. The same readings as time-series metrics in index=metrics (sourcetype ipmi:metrics, ipmi.* measure names), so thermal, fan, voltage and power trends survive retention and answer in milliseconds with mstats. 3. The System Event Log (SEL): each SEL record indexed exactly once as a separate event with sensor, event type, assertion state and raw detail preserved, so BIOS-level crashes, power faults, ECC errors, fan failures and intrusion alerts become searchable Splunk events. Why it matters: IPMI/BMC is the only observability layer that survives OS crashes, power loss, and hangs. Overheating servers, dead fans, failing PSUs, dropped redundancy and unexpected reboots happen below the OS where agents and syslog can't follow, but the BMC remembers everything. TA-IPMI closes that blind spot in minutes: install it on the host, and its BMC telemetry flows into Splunk with ready-made overview and trend dashboards. Licensing: free for personal, evaluation, and non-commercial use. Commercial/production use requires a license from the author: michael@bentleypc.com. Source available at https://github.com/bentleymi/TA-IPMI
item.dc:creator: Michael Bentley

item.title: TA-Nvidia - v1.0.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Short Description:
Free NVIDIA GPU monitoring for Splunk. Streams complete nvidia-smi telemetry, temperature, utilization, memory, power, clocks, ECC, PCIe, processes, as both JSON events and index=metrics time-series, with two dashboard packs. Passes AppInspect cloud pre-cert. Commercial use requires license.


Description:
TA-Nvidia is a free, source-available Splunk add-on that brings enterprise NVIDIA GPU observability to any Splunk instance running on hosts with NVIDIA drivers. It repeatedly captures the COMPLETE nvidia-smi state; temperature, utilization, fan speed, power draw and limits, framebuffer memory, graphics/SM/clocks, ECC errors, PCIe throughput, performance state, compute processes, vGPU, and more and indexes it two ways with zero manual configuration: 1. Full JSON events (sourcetype nvidia:smi) in index=main for deep-dive fielded search, and 2. Time-series metrics (nvidia.* metric names) in index=metrics via a metric-schema pipeline, enabling fast mstats trends and visualizations. Two pre-built dashboards ship with the app GPU Overview (per-GPU cards for temp, utilization, memory, power, clock, fan) and GPU Metrics (long-window trended charts via mstats). Why this matters: GPU-equipped servers are expensive and failure-prone. Overheating, ECC errors, clock throttling, memory exhaustion, and power-limiting silently destroy GPU workload performance (AI/ML training and inference, VDI, HPC, video/transcode). Splunk has no free, turnkey NVIDIA telemetry app, TA-Nvidia closes that gap in about one minute, on any distribution (Tested on datacenter and workstation cards, current driver: 580.x, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell). Licensing: free for personal, evaluation, and non-commercial use. Commercial/production use requires a license from the author: michael@bentleypc.com. Source is available on GitHub: https://github.com/bentleymi/TA-Nvidia

Release Notes:
# v5.2.0 Splunk stops re-sending alerts TheHive already holds, and the add-on stops retrying them. No input needs a change when you upgrade. ## Compatibility | | Minimum | Tested with | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | TheHive | 5.2.0 | 5.x | | Cortex | 3.0.0 | 4.2.0 (5.0.0 and 5.1.0) | | Splunk | 9.3 (Python 3.9 or 3.13) | Enterprise 10.6.1.1 + ES 8.4.0 | Compatible with Splunk Enterprise 10.4 to 10.6. ## New - **Notable status once sent** (alert action *Create a new alert*, optional `notable_status`): once TheHive holds the alert, the Splunk ES notable is set to this review status ID so it is not picked up again. Empty by default; ES mode only; the Splunk user needs `edit_notable_events`. ## Fixed - An alert TheHive already holds ("already exists" or HTTP 409) is no longer retried `thehive_creation_max_retry + 1` times: the add-on stops at once and logs INFO `THCA-122`. A bare 400 stays a failure. ## Upgrading - AppInspect: no failure and no error. One `check_for_custom_mako_templates` warning remains on `appserver/templates/base.html`, generated by the UCC framework. Full release notes: see `release_notes/v5.2.0.md` in the repository.

It allows to retrieve all kind of information from TheHive/Cortex and to perform actions on these instances using Splunk, from a search or from a predefined dashboard. This TA is supporting only TheHive 5. For having an app supporting TheHive 3 or 4, please check the oldest releases. It's also supporting the Cortex 3 version. item.title: Group-IB Digital Risk Protection - v1.3.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
### Highlights * **New configuration pages:** Accounts, DRP API, Proxy, Logging and Data Inputs. Accounts are checked against Group-IB when saved. * **Two data inputs:** *Violations* (confirmed violations by default) and *Typosquatting* (look-alike domain candidates), each with its own position and a Start From choice (last N days or a date). * **One event per revision** with the record's own timestamp; unchanged re-deliveries are not indexed again. The current-state store behind the dashboards holds confirmed violations only. * **Dashboards and alerts:** Overview, Violations, Typosquatting, Brands, Takedown & Approval, Action Audit, Ingestion Health; alerts for stopped collection, new confirmed violations, reactivated violations and unanswered approvals. * **Commands:** `gibdrpapprove`, `gibdrpupload`, `gibdrpbrands`, `gibdrpsubscription`, `gibdrpresync`, `gibdrpcleanup`, `gibdrploaddemo`; writes rehearse by default (`dry_run=true`) and need an administrator. ### Upgrading from 1.2.1 * Your API key is adopted on the first run of a new input that names your account's e-mail address. * Collection stops until you create a new input; the 1.2.1 input and the `gibget*`/`gibsetstatus` commands are removed. Delete the old `[drp://]` stanza from `local/inputs.conf`.


Short Description:
Splunk application that collects your Group-IB Digital Risk Protection portfolio as structured events, with dashboards that show what is true now and what changed, and commands that act on it at Group-IB


Description:
Group-IB Digital Risk Protection watches the internet for abuse of your brands — phishing pages, fake shops, counterfeit listings, impersonating social accounts, rogue mobile apps — and runs the takedowns. This application brings that portfolio into Splunk beside the rest of your security data. This Splunk integration allows you to: - Collect two feeds, each with its own data input and sourcetype: Violations (confirmed violations) and Typosquatting (look-alike domain candidates). - Keep a change history, not duplicates: one event per revision, and a current-state store that answers "what is true now" in one lookup. - Watch the portfolio on seven dashboards, and be told by six alerts — among them Group-IB DRP - Collection has stopped — when an input fails, a takedown does not hold, or Group-IB is waiting on you. - Act from the search bar: approve, reject or declare a violation with `| gibdrpapprove`, submit new ones with `| gibdrpupload`, read your brands and entitlements with `| gibdrpbrands` and `| gibdrpsubscription`, and maintain the app with `| gibdrpresync`, `| gibdrpcleanup` and `| gibdrploaddemo`. Every change sent to Group-IB is audited locally. To use this application you need an active Group-IB Digital Risk Protection subscription, a portal account with an API key, and Splunk Enterprise 9.2+ or Splunk Cloud.

item.description:

Short Description:
Configurable executive, IT operations, and secure networking dashboards unifying Cisco network health, identity, security, infrastructure, application, and topology data in Splunk.


Description:
Beta release: Participation is by invitation only and limited to a small group of approved users. The app is not yet publicly downloadable on Splunkbase, and access requests are not currently being accepted. General availability is targeted for fall 2026. Splunk App for Secure Networking helps organizations turn fragmented Cisco infrastructure, networking, identity, security, application experience, and building telemetry into clear executive and operational insights in Splunk. Cisco environments often produce data across multiple products, add-ons, indexes, sourcetypes, and data models. Building a consolidated view normally requires teams to create and maintain separate searches, dashboards, index mappings, and visualizations. This app provides a reusable foundation that brings those signals together through configurable dashboards, shared search definitions, index-mapping macros, health indicators, drilldowns, and interactive topology views. The app includes Secure Networking Posture dashboards covering Zero Trust Access, Secure Infrastructure, Scalable Network Segmentation, Hybrid Mesh Firewalling, and Agentic Operations. It also provides executive briefing, IT health, security, asset inventory, network readiness, building intelligence, Cisco Spaces, and network topology experiences. Searches use configurable index macros instead of hardcoded index names, allowing the app to adapt to different Splunk environments. Administrators can use the included Macro Index Tuning utility to discover relevant data and map dashboards to their indexes. Splunk App for Secure Networking does not collect Cisco data directly. It visualizes data already ingested into Splunk through applicable Cisco add-ons, integrations, and data models. The dashboards displayed and populated in each environment depend on the available data sources. The app is intended for network operations, security operations, IT operations, Splunk administrators, architects, customer success teams, and executives who need a consolidated view of the health, security, availability, and performance of their Cisco environment.

Release Notes:
## SCIP v1.2.18 — Role-Aware Gateway Content, Prompt-Injection Pattern Accuracy, and OSV Range Matching This release supersedes v1.2.17 and carries forty fixes and improvements across AI and LLM threat detection, vulnerability matching accuracy, and deployment documentation. No configuration changes or manual steps are required on upgrade. No detection severity value or MITRE ATLAS technique mapping changed. **AI and LLM gateway coverage:** - Kong AI Gateway request payloads are now parsed and routed by message role across all three of Kong's logging key layouts, so prompt content is separated into user, system, assistant and tool channels instead of being evaluated as one blended string. - Kong AI Gateway responses now reach the role-aware assistant channel. Three response-reading detections, including LLM Sensitive Information Disclosure, previously returned nothing at all on Kong traffic. - user_input is assembled per message role on every supported gateway, so a detection targeting user-supplied prompt content no longer matches on system or assistant text. - LiteLLM deployments behind a load balancer now attribute activity to the real caller when the documented IP-forwarding step is configured. That documented step previously had no effect and attribution fell back to the balancer. - Gateway attribution fields are normalised consistently across the supported gateways, and the gateways where a field is not yet established are recorded as such rather than assumed. **Detection accuracy:** - Six detection stanzas no longer match on bare over-broad words such as "override" and "disregard", which fired on ordinary operational text. They now match the injection shape plus a tiered set of retained literals. - Prompt-injection patterns now match every "verb + qualifier + previous instructions" phrasing rather than a fixed list of phrases. - Two detections were rewritten away from literal phrase matching to shape-based patterns. - The credential-harvesting detection no longer fires on ordinary security advice. - Repeated injection attempts by one actor within one session no longer raise duplicate alerts. - LLM Cache Poisoning can now fire, because its gate read fields the rule never received. - Two detections carried pattern alternatives that could never match. Both are corrected, with regression fixtures added. - 68 ATLAS detections now surface the confidence value they already computed, bringing all 75 that compute one to carry it through to the alert. **Vulnerability matching:** - Advisories that express several affected version ranges for one package are now matched against every range. Previously only the first range was kept, so a component inside any later range was reported as not vulnerable. - Exact affected-version lists are now read for advisories that carry no machine-readable range. - Git commit hashes are no longer presented as upgrade targets, and the fix-availability state now distinguishes "no fix published" from "fix recorded only as a commit". - The bundled vulnerability seed and the live OSV feed both now cover all eleven documented ecosystems. The seed previously drew from five and the live feed polled eight. - Repository-qualified ecosystem values no longer reach the lookup. All three writers normalise the value, and an affected install corrects itself on its next scheduled run. - Severity grading in the bundled seed is restored. The offline generator carried an older severity parser that graded roughly 90 percent of rows as unknown. - The bundled snapshot date shown on the Home dashboard is written alongside the seed, so it can no longer report a date the seed does not match. - On licensed tiers the live OSV feed hands off to the vulnerability lookup automatically once it holds data, with no manual step. The Home dashboard freshness indicator derives its state from the lookup contents and adds a "lookup behind live feed" state. **Platform and documentation:** - The vendored Splunk SDK for Python is upgraded to 3.0.1. - Supported Splunk version statements are aligned across the app and its documentation. - The air-gapped and IL deployment guides are corrected. The OSV feed is now listed in the egress-disable procedure, the customer seed refresh procedure specifies the extraction rules it previously omitted, and the stated Python requirement for the offline seed generator is corrected. **Upgrade notes:** - No manual steps, configuration changes or saved-search edits are required. - Component vulnerability counts may rise after upgrade. Advisories with several affected version ranges were previously matched against the first range only, so components inside a later range were reported as not vulnerable. Those components now match correctly. Risk scores, dashboard counts and remediation rows reflect the corrected matching. - Installs running the live OSV feed on a licensed tier correct the ecosystem value in the lookup on the next scheduled run. No licensing or crypto surface was modified in this release. bin/scip_license_core.py and bin/scip_ed25519_verify.py are byte-identical to baseline.

It prioritizes with CISA KEV and EPSS and assesses compliance posture across nine frameworks — detection logic written as transparent SPL you can open and read, and no separate platform to stand up. ### 1.6.0 #### Breaking changes in 1.6.0 Read these before upgrading from 1.5.7 or earlier. * **Splunk 10.2 or later is required.** The merge command now needs Python 3.13, which older versions cannot use for search commands. Upgrade Splunk first. * **Your merge search is updated on your first save.** After upgrading, scheduled runs keep using the old search until you save something on the Configure page (for example, change a setting and save). Run *Run preview* on the Pipeline tab before the next scheduled run to see what will change. * **You may get fewer, larger assets.** Earlier versions silently failed to join records that were far apart in a large input. They now join. * **Some data is skipped by default.** A key found in more than 50 rows is no longer used for matching, and a built-in list of placeholder values (for example `0.0.0.0`, `unknown`, `n/a`, all-zero MAC addresses) is ignored in key fields. Change both in Settings. * **Bad runs are blocked.** A run that produces fewer than half of the last run's assets is not saved, and a run with no assets never replaces the asset list. If your inventory legitimately shrinks by more than half, lower *Minimum size vs last run*. * **Multivalue fields keep the most recent values.** When a field has more values than *Max values*, it used to keep the first ones alphabetically. Short Description:
Free threat intelligence from live honeypot sensors, in SPL. Enrich any IP field with a verdict, ASN, ports and first and last seen, or query the dataset directly: raw probes, request payloads, CVE exploitation, JA4 fingerprints, top attackers. Description:
Free to use. The app and both threat feeds work without an account, and a free API key raises the daily lookup cap. HoneyLabs runs open-source honeypot sensors on the public internet. Nothing reaches them by accident, so every connection they record is a scan, a probe, a brute-force attempt or an exploit. There are no false positives to filter out, because there is no legitimate traffic to confuse them with. This app puts that dataset inside Splunk. Two search commands. The first enriches addresses you already have. Point it at any field holding a public IPv4 address and it annotates every event: index=firewall | honeylabs field=src_ip | where honeylabs_events > 0 It writes back verdict, verdict_key, network_type, events, first_seen, last_seen, country, asn, asn_org, rdns, top_port, ports, exploit_hits and reference, each prefixed honeylabs_ so nothing collides with your own fields. Addresses are de-duplicated per search, so an index carrying the same scanner across ten thousand events costs one lookup. The second queries the honeypot dataset directly, with no local data required. Nine modes cover raw events, captured request payloads, top attackers, timelines, ASN profiles, TLS and HTTP fingerprints, IOC and CIDR lookups, CVE exploitation, and fingerprint population counts. Use it to answer questions your own logs cannot: who else is exercising this CVE, what payload is being sent, which other sources share this JA4 fingerprint. Two modular inputs, shipped disabled, index active exploiter addresses and captured malware staging URLs on an hourly schedule. Neither needs credentials. Two dashboards ship with the app: an overview of what the feeds currently carry, and an explorer for querying the dataset without writing SPL by hand. About the API key. The app installs and runs with no account and no setup, but anonymous use is capped at 10 lookups a day, which is enough to try the commands and not enough to work with. A free key raises that to 500 a day and takes about a minute to create at https://honeylabs.net/dashboard. Paste it into the app's setup page; it is stored through Splunk's storage/passwords, encrypted at rest, and never written to a .conf file. Paid plans go to 50,000 a day. On privacy: a lookup sends only the public IP addresses in your search. Not your index, host, source or sourcetype names, not your Splunk version, not the search string. Private, loopback, link-local, multicast and reserved addresses are filtered out locally before the request is built. The feed inputs are ordinary HTTPS downloads of a public file and disclose nothing at all. Running Enterprise Security? Load the indicator feeds through its own threat intelligence framework so they reach correlation searches and risk scoring rather than only being searchable, and keep these commands for on-demand investigation. Description:
The Xage Fabric TA is a technical add-on that ingests and normalizes Xage Fabric syslog audit logs into Splunk's Common Information Model. The add-on parses RFC5424-formatted syslog messages containing JSON audit payloads, extracting authentication events, configuration changes, and security alerts. The add-on handles both TCP and UDP syslog inputs as well as file-based monitoring, and performs sourcetype classification at index time to ensure proper field extraction. It is designed to operate in conjunction with the companion stg_Xage app, which provides visualization dashboards and Enterprise Security correlation searches.
